board_events.text: Conditional Probability — Shrinking the World
New information doesn't change reality; it changes what we know.
Given $F$ has happened, how likely is $E$ now?
$F$ is a fact you're handed — not a second event you hope for.
Top: outcomes in both $E$ and $F$. Bottom: the reduced world, just $F$.

Independence — When Knowing Changes Nothing
Sometimes new information is completely useless.
Toss a coin, then roll a die: heads tells you nothing about the die.
$F$ shrank the world, but $E$'s share of it is unchanged.
Colony of 100 families: 30 own a car, 40 own a two-wheeler.

Independent Is NOT Mutually Exclusive
The single biggest trap in this whole topic.
Mutually exclusive: $A \cap B = \varnothing$ — one happening forbids the other.
That is the STRONGEST dependence, not independence!
Century and a duck in the same innings: mutually exclusive, far from independent.

Proof — Conditioning Shrinks the Sample Space
Claim: if $P(F) > 0$, then $P(E \mid F) = \dfrac{P(E \cap F)}{P(F)}$.
Take equally likely outcomes. Knowing $F$ occurred, the effective space is $F$ alone.
Now divide top and bottom by $n(S)$, the total number of outcomes.
Dividing by $n(S)$ turns raw counts into probabilities.
That last step is why the result holds even when outcomes aren't equally likely.
Proof — Independence Survives Complements
If $A$ and $B$ are independent, so are $A$ and $B'$.
Split $A$ by whether $B$ happens or not:
So $A$ and $B'$ are independent — a CBSE favourite.
Apply twice: $A'$ with $B$, and $A'$ with $B'$, are independent too.

The working definition — equivalent to $P(E \mid F) = P(E)$.
For three events, checking the pairs is NOT enough.
Mutual independence needs the triple product too, not just the pairs.

segments.text: <curious>Sounds simple, but this hides the whole chapter.</curious> On a Mumbai platform you guess the next train; the board flashes Western Railway and your guess sharpens. The trains didn't change — what you know did.
That's conditional probability. Information doesn't rewrite what's happening; it shrinks the possibilities you reason about down to a smaller, relevant world.
So probability of E given F asks: F has definitely occurred, and given that, how likely is E right now?
The key shift is this. F isn't a second event you also want. It's handed to you as fact, so you discard every outcome where F didn't happen.
That gives the formula: probability of E given F equals probability of E-and-F, over probability of F.
The top counts outcomes inside both E and F; the bottom is your new universe, just F. You've stopped dividing by the whole sample space.
Picture a Diwali mela. F is the food-court crowd. Told the person is there, you count jalebi-eaters among food-court people only; the rest is irrelevant.
One guard-rail: this needs probability of F above zero. You can never condition on the impossible.
Conditional probability has a twin idea, and here it is: sometimes the new information simply doesn't matter.
If knowing F leaves E exactly as likely as before, then F told you nothing useful about E. That is independence.
Toss a coin, then roll a die. Knowing the coin showed heads changes nothing about the die; the die doesn't care.
Formally, E and F are independent when probability of E given F equals the plain probability of E. The condition didn't move the number.
Notice what that means geometrically. F did shrink the world, but E's slice of that smaller world is identical to its slice of the big one.
A concrete feel. In a hundred families, thirty own a car and forty own a two-wheeler. Pick one at random and the car chance is thirty percent.
Now say twelve own both. Learn the family owns a two-wheeler: among those forty, twelve own a car, still thirty percent. Change both to eighteen and it jumps to forty-five percent.
Same setup, two different stories, decided entirely by how big the overlap is. Small overlap means independent; a larger overlap means the information starts to matter.
Here is where almost everyone stumbles, so let's nail it down right now.
Students hear 'independent' and 'mutually exclusive' and blur them together. They are nearly opposite ideas.
Mutually exclusive means the events can't both happen; their intersection is empty. If one occurs, the other is ruled out.
<excited>But that's the strongest possible dependence, not independence!</excited> One event completely controls the other's fate.
A batsman scoring a century and getting a duck in the same innings are mutually exclusive, about as far from independent as two events can get.
Visually, mutually exclusive events are two separate circles that never touch; independent events overlap by exactly the product of their probabilities.
A practical tell for exams: drawing with replacement leaves the box unchanged, so the draws are independent. Without replacement the box changes, and the draws become dependent.
The working definition of independence is the product rule: probability of E-and-F equals probability of E times probability of F.
Prefer this product form as your test. It never divides by anything, so it stays valid even when a probability is zero.
Let's prove the formula rather than just trust it. The proof is the intuition made exact.
The claim: whenever the probability of F is positive, probability of E given F equals probability of E-and-F over probability of F.
Start with equally likely outcomes. Once you know F occurred, every outcome outside F is ruled out, so your effective sample space is F alone.
Among the outcomes in F, the ones that also make E true are exactly those in E-and-F. So the conditional is the count of E-and-F over the count of F.
Here is the one clever move: divide both the top and the bottom by n of S, the total number of outcomes.
The counts become probabilities: E-and-F over F, each as a fraction of the whole. The n of S cancels, leaving our formula.
That division is the crucial step; it converts raw counts into genuine probabilities.
And because it's now written purely in probabilities, we take it as the definition even when outcomes aren't equally likely. The formula survives.
Independence has a beautiful robustness that exams exploit constantly, so let's prove it.
The claim: if A and B are independent, then A and the complement of B are also independent.
Split A cleanly by whether B happens: the part of A inside B, plus the part of A outside B.
In symbols, probability of A equals probability of A-and-B plus probability of A-and-not-B.
Rearrange, then use independence to replace probability of A-and-B with probability of A times probability of B.
Factor out probability of A, and one minus probability of B is just probability of not-B. So probability of A-and-not-B equals probability of A times probability of not-B.
That is exactly the product rule, so A and not-B are independent. C B S E loves asking this one directly.
Apply the same argument twice and you get more: A-complement with B, and A-complement with B-complement, are independent too. Independence survives every complement combination.
Now the independence formulas, plus the single most-used result in the whole chapter.
The working definition: E and F are independent exactly when probability of E-and-F equals probability of E times probability of F.
This is equivalent to saying probability of E given F equals probability of E, the condition doesn't move the number, but the product form is safer to use.
A warning for three events: verifying that the three pairs are independent is not enough on its own.
You also need the triple product: probability of A-and-B-and-C equal to the product of all three individual probabilities.
Only with all four conditions, the three pairs and the triple, do you have genuine mutual independence. J E E Advanced tests exactly this gap.
Finally, the workhorse. For 'at least one of n independent events,' never expand the union. Go through the complement, 'none of them occurs.'
So probability of at least one equals one minus the product, over all events, of one minus each event's probability.
That single trick converts an awkward union with many cross-terms into a clean product. Reach for it whenever you see 'at least one.'

board_events.text: Worked Example — Conditional on a Die (CBSE)
A fair die is rolled twice. $E$: sum is $9$. $F$: first roll exceeds $3$.
Total outcomes: $36$. $F$ means first roll in $\{4,5,6\}$.
$E \cap F$: sum $9$ with first roll above $3$ — pairs $(4,5),(5,4),(6,3)$.
$(3,6)$ is rejected — a first roll of $3$ is not greater than $3$.
Worked Example — Independent or Exclusive? (JEE Main)
$P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.4$, $P(A \cup B) = 0.7$. Classify $A$ and $B$.
Don't guess from the setup — get the intersection first.

board_events.latex: P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B)

board_events.text: Independence test: $P(A)\,P(B) = 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.2$.
Not mutually exclusive: $P(A \cap B) = 0.2 \neq 0$.
Worked Example — Picking Without Replacement (JEE Main)
Panel: $7$ boys, $5$ girls. Pick $3$ one by one, no replacement.
(i) Given the first two are girls, chance the third is a boy?
Two girls removed leaves $10$ people, of whom $7$ are boys.
(ii) Chance all three picks are girls — use the chain rule.

board_events.latex: P(G_1 \cap G_2 \cap G_3) = P(G_1)\,P(G_2 \mid G_1)\,P(G_3 \mid G_1 \cap G_2)

board_events.text: Each factor uses the shrunken pool from the pick before it.
Worked Example — Both, Neither, Exactly One (JEE Advanced)
$A$, $B$ independent. $P(\text{both}) = \tfrac{1}{8}$, $P(\text{neither}) = \tfrac{3}{8}$.
Let $P(A) = a$, $P(B) = b$. Independence gives $ab = \tfrac{1}{8}$.
So $a, b$ are roots of $8t^2 - 6t + 1 = 0$.
Exactly one occurs: $P(A) + P(B) - 2P(A \cap B)$.
Check: $\tfrac{1}{8} + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{3}{8} = 1$ — the three cases exhaust everything.
Common Pitfalls — Read Before the Exam
Pitfall 1: confusing 'mutually exclusive' with 'independent.'
Mutually exclusive with positive probabilities means strongly dependent, not independent.
Pitfall 2: flipping the conditional — $P(A \mid B) \neq P(B \mid A)$.
Umbrella given rain is high; rain given umbrella is much lower — same events.
Pitfall 3: pairwise independence does NOT imply mutual independence.
For three events, the triple product can still fail even if all pairs pass.
Pitfall 4: ignoring the given, reverting to the unconditional probability.
In 'given at least one girl,' using the plain probability throws away the condition.
Phrase-to-Symbol Decoder + Pro-Tip
Translate exam English into set notation before touching a formula.
'given that $F$ has occurred' $\to$ a conditional $P(\cdot \mid F)$.
'both $A$ and $B$' $\to P(A \cap B)$; '$A$ or $B$' $\to P(A \cup B)$.
'neither $A$ nor $B$' $\to P(A' \cap B') = 1 - P(A \cup B)$.

board_events.latex: P(\text{exactly one of } A, B) = P(A) + P(B) - 2P(A \cap B)

board_events.text: Pro-tip: compute the intersection first, then run two one-second checks.
Is $P(A \cap B) = 0$? Is $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)$?
'$= 0$' means mutually exclusive; '$= P(A)P(B)$' means independent.

segments.text: Let's run a clean Boards-level problem end to end.
A fair die is rolled twice. E is the event that the sum is nine; F is the event that the first roll shows a number greater than three.
There are thirty six equally likely outcomes. F fixes the first roll to four, five, or six.
That's three choices for the first roll and six for the second, so probability of F is eighteen over thirty six.
Now E-and-F: sum nine with the first roll above three. The pairs are four-five, five-four, and six-three.
<whisper>Watch the trap: three-six is rejected, because a first roll of three is not greater than three.</whisper> That is the mark most students drop.
So there are three good outcomes, giving probability of E-and-F equal to three over thirty six.
Divide: three over thirty six, over eighteen over thirty six, gives one over six. That is your conditional probability.
This is a classic J E E Main speed trap. One line of work saves you from a wrong reflex.
You're given probability of A is zero point five, probability of B is zero point four, and probability of A-or-B is zero point seven. Are they independent, mutually exclusive, both, or neither?
Don't panic-list cases. The move is to find probability of A-and-B first, in a single line.
Use the addition theorem: probability of A-and-B equals probability of A plus probability of B minus probability of A-or-B.
That is zero point five plus zero point four minus zero point seven, which is zero point two.
Now test independence: probability of A times probability of B is zero point five times zero point four, again zero point two.
Since probability of A-and-B equals the product, A and B are independent.

<excited>And they're not mutually exclusive!</excited> That would need the intersection to be zero, but it's zero point two. The trap is assuming exclusivity from a tidy setup; always compute the intersection first.
Here is where the chain rule earns its keep: a without-replacement selection.
A panel has seven boys and five girls. Three members are picked one after another, without replacement.
Part one: given that the first two picked are girls, what's the chance the third pick is a boy?
Once two girls are gone, ten people remain, and seven of them are boys.
By the reduced-sample-space idea, the chance the third is a boy is simply seven over ten.
Part two asks for the chance all three picks are girls. This is a job for the chain rule.
Probability of girl, then girl, then girl is probability of the first girl, times the second given the first, times the third given the first two.
That is five twelfths times four elevenths times three tenths, which simplifies to one over twenty two.

Now a full J E E Advanced build; it stitches several ideas together.
A and B are independent. The probability both occur is one eighth, and the probability neither occurs is three eighths. Find the two probabilities and the chance exactly one occurs.
Let probability of A be a and probability of B be b. Independence immediately gives a times b equals one eighth.
For 'neither,' remember the complements are also independent, so probability of neither is one minus a, times one minus b, equal to three eighths.
Expand: one, minus the sum of a and b, plus a-b, equals three eighths. Substitute a-b as one eighth and you get a plus b equals three quarters.
Now a and b are the two roots of the quadratic eight t squared minus six t plus one equals zero.
Solving, t equals six plus or minus two, over sixteen, which is one half or one quarter. So the pair is one half and one quarter.
Finally, 'exactly one occurs' is probability of A plus probability of B minus twice the probability of both.
That is three quarters minus two times one eighth, which is one half.

Pitfall one, the big one: confusing mutually exclusive with independent.
Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are strongly dependent; one happening forbids the other. That is the opposite of independence, not a version of it.
Pitfall two: flipping the conditional. Probability of A given B is generally not probability of B given A; their denominators differ.
Feel it: the chance someone carries an umbrella given it's raining is high, but the chance it's raining given they carry an umbrella is much lower. Same two events, very different numbers.
Pitfall three: assuming pairwise independence gives you mutual independence.
For three events, all three pairs can be independent and yet the triple product condition still fails. Check the triple explicitly.
Pitfall four: ignoring the information you were given, and sliding back to the unconditional probability.
In a problem that says 'given at least one girl,' quoting the plain probability throws away the very condition that defines the question.

Half the battle in probability is translating exam English into set notation before you reach for any formula.
When you see 'given that F has occurred,' or 'if it is known that F,' that's a conditional; the denominator becomes probability of F.

Ask: is the intersection zero? And is it equal to probability of A times probability of B?

If it's zero they're mutually exclusive; if it equals the product they're independent, and they can never both be yes unless a probability is zero. Write the symbols in the margin first and the right formula becomes obvious.

Partition = disjoint (no overlap) and exhaustive (covers everything).
Forward vs Backward — Bayes Is Inverse Probability
Total Probability reasons forward: cause leads to effect.
You know suppliers and spoilage rates; you predict the chance of a stale piece.
But the real question runs backward: you bit a stale piece — which supplier?
Effect back to cause. That inversion is exactly Bayes' Theorem.
A courtroom: a prior belief about each suspect, updated by a piece of evidence.
Spam filters do this millions of times a day: prior spam chance, updated per word.
An airtight alibi (prior near zero) stays innocent, however well the evidence fits.

Your gut blames the worst spoilage rate — but volume matters too.
A 95%-accurate test for a rare disease can still leave a positive patient likely healthy.

segments.text: Let's meet the engine of this subtopic through a Diwali sweet shop.
A mithai shop sources its kaju katli from three suppliers: A ships fifty percent of the stock, B thirty percent, and C twenty percent.
Each supplier occasionally sends a stale piece. You walk in and pick a random box. What's the chance it's stale?
No single supplier's spoilage rate answers this, because the box could have come from any of them.
So you weight each supplier's spoilage rate by how much stock they contribute, and add it all up. That weighted sum is the Theorem of Total Probability.
Picture it as three stock segments; each contributes its share times its spoilage rate, and the total stale chance is the sum of those contributions.
In symbols, the probability of the effect A is the sum, over every cause, of the cause's prior times the effect's likelihood under that cause.
For this to work, the suppliers must form a partition: every box comes from exactly one supplier, and from some supplier.
That's the two-word requirement: disjoint, so the causes never overlap, and exhaustive, so together they cover every possibility.
<curious>Total Probability and Bayes are two directions of the same machinery</curious> — let's separate them.
Total Probability reasons forward, from cause to effect.
You know the suppliers and their spoilage rates, and you predict the chance of a stale piece. Cause first, effect second.
But the interesting exam questions run the film backward. You've already bitten into a stale piece; now, which supplier most likely sent it?
That backward question, from observed effect to hidden cause, is exactly what Bayes' Theorem answers. It inverts the direction of conditioning, which is why it's called inverse probability.

A courtroom captures the spirit. Before any evidence, the judge holds a prior belief about each suspect. A fingerprint arrives, and belief updates toward whoever best fits both plausibility and evidence.
Spam filters run the same loop millions of times a day: a prior chance that a message is spam, updated by the likelihood of each word it contains.
And a crucial point: a suspect with an airtight alibi, a prior near zero, stays innocent no matter how well the evidence fits. That's why some causes simply drop out.
Now the trap your intuition sets, and the single biggest reason Bayes surprises people.
Your gut screams that the culprit is whoever has the worst spoilage rate. But if that supplier barely ships anything, sheer volume from a cleaner supplier can make it the likelier source.
The classic version is medical. <excited>A test that's ninety five percent accurate for a rare disease can still leave a patient who tested positive far more likely to be healthy than sick!</excited>
Three names to hold: the prior is the base rate, the likelihood is the test's accuracy, and the posterior is your updated belief after seeing the result.
Why the surprise? Healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones, so even a small false-positive rate, applied to that huge pool, produces a flood of false positives.
Picture everyone who tests positive: only a thin slice are truly carriers; the rest are false alarms from the large healthy majority.
Bayes forces you to respect both numbers, the prior and the likelihood, instead of chasing the scary accuracy figure alone.
A practical consequence: if your posteriors ever fail to sum to one, you've used a non-partition or divided by the wrong denominator.
That error is structural, not arithmetic, so re-examine your cases before you re-check your sums.
Let's prove Total Probability — it's short, and it shows exactly where each partition property is used.
Because the causes are exhaustive, their union is the whole sample space, so every outcome of A falls into one of them.
That lets us slice A along the partition: A is the union, over all causes, of A-and-that-cause.
These pieces are pairwise disjoint, because the causes themselves are disjoint. No two of them share an outcome.
And for a disjoint union, probabilities simply add: probability of A is the sum of probability of A-and-each-cause.
Now rewrite each piece with the multiplication theorem from the last subtopic: probability of A-and-a-cause is the cause's prior times the likelihood of A under it.
Substituting gives the theorem: probability of A equals the sum, over all causes, of prior times likelihood.
So the two partition properties each earn their keep: exhaustive lets us split A into the union, and disjoint lets us add the probabilities with no overlap corrections.
Bayes' Theorem falls out of two things you already have: the definition of conditional probability and Total Probability.
Start from the definition, applied to the conditional we actually want, the cause given the evidence.
Probability of cause E-i given A is probability of E-i-and-A over probability of A.
For the numerator, use the multiplication theorem the convenient way round, conditioning on the cause, whose likelihood we actually know.
That makes the numerator the cause's prior times the likelihood of A under that cause.
For the denominator, substitute Total Probability, the full sum over all causes.
Putting the two together gives Bayes' Theorem: prior times likelihood on top, and the total probability of the evidence on the bottom.

The physical idea: we're handed the likelihoods, effect given cause, but we want the posteriors, cause given effect. Bayes is the bridge that flips the direction, and Total Probability builds its denominator.

Posteriors sum to one — a free consistency check.
Priors also sum to one; if they don't, you don't have a partition.
If the posteriors miss one, suspect a non-partition or the wrong denominator.
Worked Example — Which Bag? (CBSE)
Bag I: $4$ red, $6$ blue. Bag II: $7$ red, $3$ blue. Pick a bag, draw one — it's red.
Causes: Bag I or Bag II, each prior $\tfrac{1}{2}$. Effect $A$: a red ball.
Check: $P(\text{Bag II} \mid \text{red}) = \tfrac{7}{11}$, and $\tfrac{4}{11} + \tfrac{7}{11} = 1$.
The red ball is likelier from Bag II, which is richer in red.
Equal priors, so the posteriors just reflect the likelihood ratio.
Worked Example — The 95% Test Trap (JEE Main)
$2\%$ carry a condition. Test flags a carrier $95\%$, a non-carrier $10\%$. Result: positive.
Don't answer 95% — that's a likelihood, not the posterior.
False positives from the huge healthy pool swamp the true positives.
Base rate wins: about 16%, not 95% — the hallmark Bayes surprise.
Worked Example — Two White Balls (JEE Main)
A: 3W,2B. B: 1W,4B. C: 4W,1B. Pick a box, draw $2$ together — both white.
Priors $\tfrac{1}{3}$ each. Effect $W$: both drawn balls white. Use combinations.
Box B contributes zero — it can't yield two whites at all.
Combinations supply the likelihoods; Bayes does the rest.

segments.text: <curious>Here's the device that turns any messy Bayes problem into bookkeeping:</curious> the probability tree.
Every Total-Probability or Bayes question can be drawn as a two-level tree, and the tree is the formula made visible.
From a single root, branches fan out to the causes, each labelled with its prior. From every cause, two more branches lead to 'A occurs' and 'A fails,' labelled with the likelihoods.
Each complete path from root to a leaf multiplies the labels along it, and that product is prior times likelihood.
So each 'A occurs' path carries probability equal to the cause's prior times the likelihood of A under that cause.
Total Probability is simply the sum of all the 'A occurs' path-products.
And Bayes asks: out of that total, what fraction travelled through cause E-i? That's the single path-product divided by the sum of the A-paths.
Draw the tree first. Because you literally add up the paths you drew, the denominator becomes impossible to get wrong.
One special case deserves its own slot, because it's the form Boards ask most.
When there are just two causes, an event E and its complement E-prime, Bayes collapses neatly.
The posterior for E is prior times likelihood for E, over prior times likelihood for E plus the same product for E-prime.
This is the disease-test and single-bag template. Recognise it and you can write the answer in a single line.
And here's a gift the structure gives you: the posteriors over any partition must sum to one.
Use that as a free consistency check at the end of every Bayes problem.
The priors must also sum to one; if they don't, what you have isn't a partition at all.
So if your posteriors miss one, don't just re-add. Suspect a non-partition or the wrong denominator, which are structural mistakes.
A clean Boards Bayes problem: the two-bag template you'll see again and again.
Bag one holds four red and six blue balls; bag two holds seven red and three blue. You pick a bag at random and draw one ball, and it turns out red.
The causes are bag one chosen and bag two chosen, each with prior one half. The observed effect is a red ball.
The likelihoods: probability of red from bag one is four tenths; from bag two it's seven tenths.
Total probability of red is one half times four tenths, plus one half times seven tenths, which is eleven twentieths.
Bayes for bag one: one half times four tenths, over eleven twentieths, which simplifies to four elevenths.
Check the partition: probability of bag two given red is seven elevenths, and four elevenths plus seven elevenths is one.
The red ball is likelier to have come from bag two, which is richer in red.
And since the priors were equal, the posteriors simply reflect the ratio of the likelihoods.
A textbook base-rate problem, and a classic J E E Main speed trap.
Two percent of people carry a condition. The test flags a carrier ninety five percent of the time, and wrongly flags a non-carrier ten percent of the time. Someone tests positive.
<whisper>Don't reach for ninety five percent — that's a likelihood, not the posterior.</whisper>
Set the priors: probability of carrier is zero point zero two, probability of non-carrier is zero point nine eight.
The likelihoods: probability of positive given carrier is zero point nine five; positive given non-carrier is zero point one zero.
Total probability of a positive: zero point zero two times zero point nine five, plus zero point nine eight times zero point one zero, which is zero point one one seven.
Posterior: zero point zero one nine over zero point one one seven, about zero point one six.
The huge non-carrier pool produces a flood of false positives that swamps the true positives.
So the base rate wins: about sixteen percent, not ninety five. That's the hallmark Bayes surprise.
Now Bayes fused with a bit of counting, a favourite J E E Main multi-concept.

Three identical boxes. Box A has three white and two black; box B has one white and four black; box C has four white and one black. You pick a box at random and draw two balls together, and both are white.
Priors are one third each. The effect W is both drawn balls white, and we get each likelihood using combinations.
For box A: choose two whites from three, over choose two from five, which is three tenths.
Box B gives zero, since you can't choose two whites from one; box C gives choose two from four, over ten, which is six tenths.
Total probability of two whites is one third times the sum three tenths plus zero plus six tenths, which is three tenths.
Bayes for box C: one third times six tenths, over three tenths, which is two thirds.
Notice box B contributes exactly zero; it simply can't produce two whites.
So combinations supply the likelihoods and Bayes does the rest, counting and probability working together.

board_events.text: Worked Example — Three Production Lines (JEE Advanced)
L1: $60\%$ output, $2\%$ defects. L2: $25\%$, $4\%$. L3: $15\%$, $8\%$. An item is defective.
Causes L1, L2, L3 partition output. Effect D: defective. Build joint = prior times likelihood.

board_events.latex: P(L_1 \mid D) = \tfrac{6}{17}, \ P(L_2 \mid D) = \tfrac{5}{17}, \ P(L_3 \mid D) = \tfrac{6}{17}

board_events.text: L1 and L3 are tied as the likeliest source, though L3 is four times as defect-prone.
High volume at a low defect rate is just as guilty as low volume at a high rate.
Common Pitfalls — Total Probability & Bayes
Pitfall 1: base-rate neglect — quoting the likelihood as the posterior.
The test's accuracy is not the probability you have the disease.
Pitfall 2: inverting the conditional — $P(A \mid E_i)$ is given, $P(E_i \mid A)$ is wanted.
They point in opposite directions; swapping them skips Bayes entirely.
Pitfall 3: a non-partition — causes that overlap or leave gaps.
If the priors don't sum to one, Total Probability silently fails.
Pitfall 4: wrong denominator — dividing by one term, not the full sum.
Bayes' denominator is always the total probability of the evidence.
Pro-Tips — The Table and the Chain
Build one row per cause: prior, likelihood, and their product.
Sum the product column — that sum is your denominator, the probability of the evidence.
This makes the full 5–6 mark Board solution almost mechanical.
Advanced: when evidence arrives in stages, today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior.
Chain the updates — don't restart from scratch for the second observation.
Final check every time: the posteriors must add up to one.
Random Variable — Turning Outcomes into Numbers
Watch one T20 over: how many runs? $0$, maybe $6$, maybe an unlikely $36$.
You mapped a messy experiment to a single real number.
A random variable X is a function: outcome in, real number out.
Heads in three tosses, defective bulbs, customers in an hour — all random variables.
The values can be listed one by one, so these are discrete random variables.
Listing the values is always the first move — you can't build a distribution without them.
Naming X is how we tame an unpredictable situation into arithmetic.
The Probability Distribution — a Fingerprint
List every value X can take with the probability of each.
It's a two-row table: values on top, probabilities below.

board_events.latex: \begin{array}{c|cccc} X & x_1 & x_2 & \cdots & x_n \\ \hline P & p_1 & p_2 & \cdots & p_n \end{array}

board_events.text: Iron rule 1: every probability lies between $0$ and $1$.
Iron rule 2: probabilities sum to exactly one — something must happen.
To find an unknown constant, impose sum = 1 and reject any negative probability.

A workshop runs three lines. Line one makes sixty percent of output with a two percent defect rate; line two, twenty five percent with four percent; line three, fifteen percent with eight percent. An item is found defective.
The three lines partition the output. The effect D is defective. Build the joint probability for each, prior times likelihood.
Line one: zero point six times zero point zero two is zero point zero one two.
Line two gives zero point zero one zero, and line three gives zero point zero one two.

Naming X is how we tame an unpredictable situation and turn it into clean arithmetic.
Once you have a random variable, the natural question is: how are its values distributed?

board_events.text: Mean = Expectation = Balance Point
The mean is a probability-weighted average, not a plain average.
Lucky-dip: $90\%$ win ₹$10$, $10\%$ win ₹$100$. Naive average says ₹$55$.
But almost nobody wins the big prize — that figure is wildly optimistic.
Weighted by how often each occurs, the honest expected prize is ₹19.

board_events.text: Variance is the average squared distance of values from the mean.
Why square? Signed deviations always cancel to zero.
Squaring kills the sign and penalises far values more heavily.
The square root returns us to the original units of X.
Derivation — the Computational Form of Variance
Start from the definition and expand the square inside the expectation.
Expectation distributes across a sum; constants pull out.
Now use $E(X) = \mu$.
One table pass gives both sums, then combine — far fewer decimal slips.
Derivation — Linear Transformations
Let $Y = aX + b$. Then the mean shifts and scales.
The $+b$ cancels itself out inside the square.
A pure shift b moves the mean but never the spread.
The scale factor a enters variance squared.
Worked Example — Three Coin Tosses (CBSE)
Fair coin tossed $3$ times. $X$ = number of heads. Values $0,1,2,3$.
So mean 3/2, variance 3/4, SD about 0.87.
Mean 1.5 isn't a value X takes — perfectly normal for an average.

segments.text: A full distribution table is bulky, so we summarise it with a single centre number: the mean, also called the expectation.
The crucial word is weighted. The mean is not a plain average of the listed values; it's a probability-weighted average, so values that occur more often pull it toward themselves.
In symbols, mu equals E of X equals the sum of each value times its probability.
Feel why the weights matter. A lucky-dip: ninety percent of tickets win ten rupees, ten percent win a hundred. A naive average of the prizes says fifty five rupees.
But almost nobody wins the hundred, so fifty five is wildly optimistic. The plain average ignored how rare the big prize is.
<excited>The honest expected prize weights each value by how often it occurs: zero point nine times ten, plus zero point one times a hundred, which is nineteen rupees!</excited>
That nineteen is the mean, and it's exactly what a fair ticket price would be in the long run. Probabilities are the weights; ignore them and the mean is meaningless.
Picture a beam with a weight equal to each probability placed at each value; the mean is the one point where the beam balances.
And notice it need not sit at any value X actually takes. The balance point of a fair-coin count can be one point five, a number of heads you never literally see.
The mean tells you the centre, but two variables with the same centre can feel completely different. That's what variance measures.
Cricket gives the perfect picture. Two batsmen can share the same average yet play nothing alike: one grinds out forty every innings, the other alternates a golden duck and a blazing century.
Same mean, wildly different spread. Variance is the number that captures that spread.
Concretely, variance is the average squared distance of the values from the mean.
In symbols, sigma squared is the sum of each squared deviation from mu, weighted by its probability.

Why square the deviations? Because a natural first attempt, the average signed deviation, is always exactly zero: the values above the mean cancel the values below it. That's literally what makes mu the balance point.
Squaring kills the sign so nothing cancels, and it also penalises far-flung values more heavily. A value twice as far from the mean contributes four times as much.
Taking the square root at the end gives the standard deviation, sigma.
That square root simply returns us to the original units of X, which is why standard deviation is often the more interpretable spread.
The definition of variance is honest but slow. Let's derive the faster computational form.
Start from the definition and expand the square inside the expectation: X minus mu, all squared, is X squared minus two mu X plus mu squared.
So sigma squared equals the expectation of that whole expression.
Expectation distributes across a sum, and constants pull outside, exactly like a weighted sum does.
That gives expectation of X squared, minus two mu times expectation of X, plus mu squared.
Now use the fact that expectation of X is mu itself.
The middle and last terms collapse, leaving sigma squared equals expectation of X squared minus mu squared.

Why this matters: instead of subtracting mu from every value first, you accumulate the sum of x-p and the sum of x-squared-p in a single table pass, then combine once at the end. Far fewer decimal slips.
One more derivation, and it saves you a whole second table in exams: how mean and variance behave under a linear change.
Let Y be a times X plus b. We want the mean and variance of Y.
The mean is easy: expectation of a X plus b equals a times expectation of X, plus b. The shift and scale pass straight through.
For the variance, write it as the expectation of Y minus its mean, squared. Y's mean is a mu plus b, so inside the bracket you get a X plus b minus a mu minus b.
The plus b and minus b cancel, leaving a times the quantity X minus mu.
Square that and pull the a out: variance of a X plus b is a squared times variance of X.
So a pure shift, the plus b, moves the mean but never touches the spread. Sliding all your data sideways changes the average, not how scattered it is.
And the scale factor a enters variance squared: double the variable and the variance quadruples.
The Boards classic: build a distribution, then its mean and variance.
A fair coin is tossed three times, and X is the number of heads. X can be zero, one, two, or three.
With eight equally likely outcomes, the probabilities are one eighth, three eighths, three eighths, one eighth.
Always check first: one eighth plus three eighths plus three eighths plus one eighth is one.
The mean: zero times one eighth, plus one times three eighths, plus two times three eighths, plus three times one eighth, which is twelve eighths, or three halves.
For expectation of X squared, square each value: one times three eighths, plus four times three eighths, plus nine times one eighth, which is twenty four eighths, or three.
Variance is expectation of X squared minus mu squared: three minus nine quarters, which is three quarters.
So the mean is three halves, the variance is three quarters, and the standard deviation is about zero point eight seven.
Notice the mean, one point five, isn't a value X ever takes. That's perfectly normal: it's the long-run average number of heads per three tosses.

The crucial word is weighted. The mean is not a plain average of the listed values; it's a probability-weighted average, so values that occur more often pull it toward themselves.
In symbols, mu equals E of X equals the sum of each value times its probability.
Feel why the weights matter. A lucky-dip: ninety percent of tickets win ten rupees, ten percent win a hundred. A naive average of the prizes says fifty five rupees.
But almost nobody wins the hundred, so fifty five is wildly optimistic. The plain average ignored how rare the big prize is.
<excited>The honest expected prize weights each value by how often it occurs: zero point nine times ten, plus zero point one times a hundred, which is nineteen rupees!</excited>
That nineteen is the mean, and it's exactly what a fair ticket price would be in the long run. Probabilities are the weights; ignore them and the mean is meaningless.
Picture a beam with a weight equal to each probability placed at each value; the mean is the one point where the beam balances.
And notice it need not sit at any value X actually takes. The balance point of a fair-coin count can be one point five, a number of heads you never literally see.
The mean tells you the centre, but two variables with the same centre can feel completely different. That's what variance measures.
Cricket gives the perfect picture. Two batsmen can share the same average yet play nothing alike: one grinds out forty every innings, the other alternates a golden duck and a blazing century.
Same mean, wildly different spread. Variance is the number that captures that spread.
Concretely, variance is the average squared distance of the values from the mean.
In symbols, sigma squared is the sum of each squared deviation from mu, weighted by its probability.

Why square the deviations? Because a natural first attempt, the average signed deviation, is always exactly zero: the values above the mean cancel the values below it. That's literally what makes mu the balance point.
Squaring kills the sign so nothing cancels, and it also penalises far-flung values more heavily. A value twice as far from the mean contributes four times as much.
Taking the square root at the end gives the standard deviation, sigma.
That square root simply returns us to the original units of X, which is why standard deviation is often the more interpretable spread.
The definition of variance is honest but slow. Let's derive the faster computational form.
Start from the definition and expand the square inside the expectation: X minus mu, all squared, is X squared minus two mu X plus mu squared.
So sigma squared equals the expectation of that whole expression.
Expectation distributes across a sum, and constants pull outside, exactly like a weighted sum does.
That gives expectation of X squared, minus two mu times expectation of X, plus mu squared.
Now use the fact that expectation of X is mu itself.
The middle and last terms collapse, leaving sigma squared equals expectation of X squared minus mu squared.

Why this matters: instead of subtracting mu from every value first, you accumulate the sum of x-p and the sum of x-squared-p in a single table pass, then combine once at the end. Far fewer decimal slips.
One more derivation, and it saves you a whole second table in exams: how mean and variance behave under a linear change.
Let Y be a times X plus b. We want the mean and variance of Y.
The mean is easy: expectation of a X plus b equals a times expectation of X, plus b. The shift and scale pass straight through.
For the variance, write it as the expectation of Y minus its mean, squared. Y's mean is a mu plus b, so inside the bracket you get a X plus b minus a mu minus b.
The plus b and minus b cancel, leaving a times the quantity X minus mu.
Square that and pull the a out: variance of a X plus b is a squared times variance of X.
So a pure shift, the plus b, moves the mean but never touches the spread. Sliding all your data sideways changes the average, not how scattered it is.
And the scale factor a enters variance squared: double the variable and the variance quadruples.
The Boards classic: build a distribution, then its mean and variance.
A fair coin is tossed three times, and X is the number of heads. X can be zero, one, two, or three.
With eight equally likely outcomes, the probabilities are one eighth, three eighths, three eighths, one eighth.
Always check first: one eighth plus three eighths plus three eighths plus one eighth is one.
The mean: zero times one eighth, plus one times three eighths, plus two times three eighths, plus three times one eighth, which is twelve eighths, or three halves.
For expectation of X squared, square each value: one times three eighths, plus four times three eighths, plus nine times one eighth, which is twenty four eighths, or three.
Variance is expectation of X squared minus mu squared: three minus nine quarters, which is three quarters.
So the mean is three halves, the variance is three quarters, and the standard deviation is about zero point eight seven.
Notice the mean, one point five, isn't a value X ever takes. That's perfectly normal: it's the long-run average number of heads per three tosses.

board_events.text: Worked Example — Fast Variance (JEE Main)
The trap: grinding out squared deviations with decimals.
So variance 0.49, SD 0.7 — one table pass, one subtraction.
The computational form scales painlessly to five or six values.
Worked Example — Number of Aces (JEE Main)
Draw $2$ cards together from $52$. $X$ = number of aces. Values $0,1,2$.
Mean about 0.154 aces per two-card draw.
Sanity: each card is an ace with chance $\tfrac{1}{13}$, so $2 \times \tfrac{1}{13} = \tfrac{2}{13}$.
Common Pitfalls — Random Variables
Pitfall 1: plain average instead of the probability-weighted mean.
The mean must weight each value by its probability, not divide by n.
Pitfall 2: forgetting to square the mean in variance.
Variance is E(X²) minus [E(X)]², not E(X²) minus E(X).
Pitfall 3: confusing variance with standard deviation.
SD is the square root of variance and carries the same units as X.
Pitfall 4: skipping the sum-to-one check, or accepting a negative probability.
Pitfall 5: using a formula-defined P without first finding the constant.
Pro-Tip — the Four-Column Table
Set up columns: value, probability, value×prob, value²×prob.

Bernoulli Trial — the Atom of the Topic
A penalty kick: goal or miss, with a fixed conversion chance, say 0.8.
One trial, exactly two outcomes, a fixed success probability p.
Coin toss, bulb tested, student pass/fail, one archer's arrow — all Bernoulli trials.
'Success' is just a label for the outcome you're counting.
Drawing a defective item counts as 'success' if defectives are what you want.
Repeat this identical trial and the counting story begins.

segments.text: A speed-focused problem: the point is method, not difficulty.
X takes one, two, three with probabilities zero point two, zero point five, zero point three. Find the variance.
<whisper>The trap is to grind out the sum of squared deviations with decimals — slow and slip-prone.</whisper>
Instead, one table pass. The mean is one times zero point two, plus two times zero point five, plus three times zero point three, which is two point one.
Expectation of X squared is one times zero point two, plus four times zero point five, plus nine times zero point three, which is four point nine.
Variance is four point nine minus two point one squared, that's four point nine minus four point four one, which is zero point four nine.
So the variance is zero point four nine and the standard deviation is zero point seven, from a single sweep and one subtraction.

The long route gives the same answer but with three subtractions and three squarings of awkward decimals. The computational form scales painlessly to five or six values, where the deviation form becomes a minefield.
A distribution built with combinations, then its mean, a favourite J E E Main crossover.
Draw two cards together from a standard deck of fifty two. X is the number of aces, so X is zero, one, or two.
Total ways to draw two cards is fifty two choose two, which is one thousand three hundred twenty six. There are four aces and forty eight non-aces.
Probability of zero aces is forty eight choose two, over that total, which reduces to one hundred eighty eight over two hundred twenty one.

Probability of one ace is four choose one times forty eight choose one, over the total, giving thirty two over two hundred twenty one; and two aces is four choose two over the total, which is one over two hundred twenty one.
Check the sum: one hundred eighty eight plus thirty two plus one, over two hundred twenty one, is one.
The mean is one times thirty two over two twenty one, plus two times one over two twenty one, which is thirty four over two twenty one, or two thirteenths.
So on average about zero point one five aces per two-card draw.
A neat sanity check: each single card is an ace with chance one thirteenth, so over two cards the mean count is two times one thirteenth, which is two thirteenths. It matches.
Five traps quietly cost marks on random-variable questions, so let's name them.
Pitfall one: taking a plain average instead of the probability-weighted mean.
The mean must weight each value by its probability; you never simply divide the sum of the values by n.
Pitfall two: forgetting to square the mean in the variance formula.
Variance is expectation of X squared minus the square of expectation of X, not minus expectation of X itself. The subtracted term is the mean squared.
Pitfall three: confusing variance with standard deviation.
Standard deviation is the square root of variance, and it carries the same units as X. Report whichever the question actually asks for.
Pitfall four: skipping the sum-to-one check, or accepting a value of the constant that yields a negative probability.

Pitfall five: with a formula-defined distribution like k x or c x squared, plugging in values before finding the constant. Always solve for the constant first, then confirm every probability is legal.
Close the subtopic with the one layout that makes every mean-and-variance question mechanical.
Set up four columns: the value, its probability, the value times its probability, and the value squared times its probability.
Fill one row per value: x-i, then p-i, then x-i p-i, then x-i squared p-i.
Sum the third column to get expectation of X; sum the fourth to get expectation of X squared.
Then variance is the fourth-column sum minus the square of the third-column sum, in one final line.
A bonus: the probability column summing to one is your built-in validity check, done before you even reach the mean.
This single-pass table converts any mean or variance question into plain arithmetic, and it scales to five or six values without fuss.
<whisper>And the sanity check that never fails: variance can never be negative. If it comes out negative, you dropped the square on mu.</whisper>
This is also exactly the layout that earns full method marks in Boards, because every step is visible and organised.
<curious>Think of a penalty shootout — what are the possible outcomes of a single kick?</curious>
Just two: goal or miss. And a striker of fixed quality converts with some steady probability, say zero point eight, on every attempt.
A single two-outcome attempt with a fixed success probability is a Bernoulli trial: the atom of this whole topic.
One coin toss, one bulb tested for a defect, one student passing or failing, one archer's single arrow — each is a Bernoulli trial the moment we call one result success and the other failure.
We write the success probability as p, and the failure probability as q, which is simply one minus p.
And a key subtlety: success is just a label for the outcome you're counting. It need not be anything good.
So drawing a defective item is a perfectly valid success when defectives are exactly what you want to count.
Now repeat this identical trial many times, and the counting story of the binomial distribution begins.

sections.title: The binomial distribution: counting successes & related topics

board_events.text: The Binomial Distribution — Counting Successes
Repeat the kick n times: how many goals? That count is a random variable.
Its distribution is the binomial distribution.
To get r successes: pick which r trials succeed, then have the rest fail.
Defectives in a carton, sixes in dice rolls, correct guesses — all fit this mould.
Read it: choose the successes, power up p, power down with q for the failures.
The surface stories differ; the skeleton is identical.
The Four Conditions for Binomial
1. A finite, fixed number of trials, n.
2. The trials are independent.
3. Each trial has exactly two outcomes.
4. The success probability p stays constant.
Strip away any one condition and the binomial formula no longer applies.
Classic violation: drawing without replacement — the deck's composition shifts.
Without replacement, p drifts trial to trial — not binomial. Replace, and it is.
Shape, Mode, and Variance < Mean

$p < 0.5$ leans to lower counts (right-skewed).
The peak sits at the mode, near np; mean and mode need not coincide.

Two binomials with $p$ and $1 - p$ are mirror images of each other.
Derivation — Mean np and Variance npq
Use the identity $r \cdot \binom{n}{r} = n \cdot \binom{n-1}{r-1}$.
The index shift collapses the sum to $(q + p)^{n-1} = 1$.
For variance, first compute E[X(X-1)] = n(n-1)p².
Concrete check B(2, ½): mean 1, variance ½ — matches np and npq.
Read mean and variance straight off n and p — no table needed.
Worked Example — Exactly Two Sixes (CBSE)
A fair die is rolled $5$ times. Find $P(\text{exactly 2 sixes})$.
Success = a six, so $p = \tfrac16$, $q = \tfrac56$; $n = 5$, $r = 2$.

List r = 0,1,...,5 and compute only the few you need.

segments.text: Now repeat the kick n times under identical conditions and ask the natural question: how many goals?
That count, the number of successes in n independent, identical Bernoulli trials, is itself a random variable.
Its distribution is the binomial distribution, the single most important named distribution in school probability.
Here's how the formula is built. To get exactly r successes, you must do two things: pick which r of the n trials succeed, and then have those succeed while the rest fail.
The number of ways to pick which r trials are the successes is n choose r.

Each such arrangement has probability p to the r times q to the n minus r, because the trials are independent. Multiply, and probability of X equals r is n choose r, times p to the r, times q to the n minus r.
Defectives in a carton of twenty, sixes in a string of dice rolls, correct answers from pure guessing, rainy days in a week — all of them fit this mould.
Read the formula in three pieces: choose the successes with n choose r, power up p for the r successes, and power down with q for the n minus r failures.
The surface stories differ wildly, but strip them down and the skeleton is identical: count the successes in n fixed, independent, equal-probability yes-no trials.
Four conditions must hold for a sequence of trials to be Bernoulli, and hence for the count to be binomial.
One: there is a finite, fixed number of trials, called n. You know in advance how many there are.
Two: the trials are independent. What happens on one trial doesn't influence any other.
Three: each trial has exactly two outcomes, success and failure.
Four: the success probability p stays constant across every trial.
Strip away any one of these four and the binomial formula no longer applies.
The classic violation is drawing without replacement. Pull cards one by one and the composition of the deck changes.

So p drifts from trial to trial and the draws become dependent — not binomial. Replace the card each time and it becomes binomial again. Whenever you see without replacement, your binomial antenna should switch off.
It pays to picture the shape of a binomial distribution before you compute, because the picture catches gross errors.
Here's the distribution for six trials with success probability zero point eight. The bars rise to a clear peak at five, with the mean sitting a little lower at four point eight.
When p equals one half, the binomial is perfectly symmetric. When p is above one half, it leans toward higher counts, which we call left-skewed.
When p is below one half, it leans toward lower counts, or right-skewed.
<excited>The peak sits at the mode, near n times p — and notice the mode and the mean need not be the same value!</excited>
A permanent identity: the variance, n p q, is always strictly less than the mean, n p, because q is less than one.
So if a problem ever hands you a binomial whose variance is larger than its mean, the data is inconsistent — a favourite trap.
A couple of structural facts: a binomial on n trials has exactly n plus one possible values, zero through n.
And two binomials with the same n but success probabilities p and one minus p are perfect mirror images of each other.
The mean and variance of a binomial can be read straight off n and p. Here's why, in brief.
For the mean, start from the sum of r times the binomial term, and use the identity r times n choose r equals n times n minus one choose r minus one.
That identity pulls an n p outside the sum.
The leftover sum is just a smaller binomial expansion, q plus p to the n minus one, which equals one. So the expectation of X is n p.
For the variance, the neat route is to first compute the expectation of X times X minus one, which works out to n times n minus one, times p squared, by the same index shift done twice.
Then variance equals that expectation of X times X minus one, plus the expectation of X, minus the square of the expectation of X.
Substituting gives n n-minus-one p squared, plus n p, minus n p all squared, which simplifies cleanly to n p q.
A concrete check with two fair-coin tosses: the mean is one and the variance is one half, and those match n p and n p q exactly.
So the shortcuts aren't magic; they're the table calculation done once and for all. Read mean and variance straight off n and p.
A clean Boards binomial: exactly r successes.
A fair die is rolled five times, and we want the probability of getting exactly two sixes.
Each roll is a Bernoulli trial. Call a six a success, so p is one sixth and q is five sixths; n is five and r is two.
By the formula, probability of exactly two is five choose two, times one sixth squared, times five sixths cubed.

That's ten times one thirty sixth times one hundred twenty five over two hundred sixteen, which is six hundred twenty five over three thousand eight hundred eighty eight, about zero point one six one.
A common follow-up asks for at most one six, which is probability of zero plus probability of one.
That's five sixths to the fifth, plus five choose one times one sixth times five sixths to the fourth.
The two pieces are three thousand one hundred twenty five each, over seven thousand seven hundred seventy six, giving six thousand two hundred fifty over that, about zero point eight zero four.
The standard Board layout is to list the counts zero through five and compute only the few probabilities you actually need.

sections.title: Worked example: at least one defective (JEE Main) & Pitfalls

board_events.text: Worked Example — At Least One Defective (JEE Main)
$5\%$ of items defective. Sample of $10$. Find $P(\text{at least one})$.
'At least one' = complement of 'none' — never sum ten terms.
Variance 0.475 < mean 0.5, as it must be.
Even a 5% rate gives about a 40% chance of catching one in ten.
Worked Example — Recover n and p (JEE Main)
Mean and variance of a binomial are $4$ and $2$. Find $n$, $p$, $P(X=2)$.
Two numbers pin a binomial completely — divide to get q.
Cross-check: $npq = 8 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = 2$, variance $<$ mean.
Divide variance by mean first — that's the whole trick.
Worked Example — Most Probable Hits (JEE Advanced)
Archer hits with $p = 0.8$, fires $6$ shots. Find the mode and its probability.
The mean is np = 4.8, yet the single most likely count is 5.
Mean and mode need not coincide.
The mode comes from the ratio of consecutive probabilities.
Common Pitfalls — Binomial Distribution
Pitfall 1: forcing binomial onto without-replacement (dependent) trials.
There p shifts each draw, so it is not binomial.
Pitfall 2: swapping $p$ and $q$, or $r$ and $n - r$.
Successes get p to the r; failures get q to the n − r.
Pitfall 3: believing variance can exceed the mean.
For a binomial, npq is always less than np.
Pitfall 4: the long road to 'at least one' instead of $1 - q^n$.
Pitfall 5: dropping or miscounting the nCr factor.
Pro-Tips — Three Reflexes
Any 'at least' or 'at most' should trigger the complement reflex.
For 'mean and variance given,' divide variance by mean first.
For several consecutive probabilities, compute P(0) once, then walk up.
Each next probability is the previous one times a simple factor.

segments.text: A J E E Main speed trap built on the at-least-one reflex.
In a production run, five percent of items are defective. A random sample of ten is taken. Find the probability that at least one is defective, and state the mean and variance.
<whisper>At least one is the complement of none — never sum ten separate terms.</whisper>
So probability of at least one is one minus probability of zero defectives, which is one minus ten choose zero times zero point zero five to the zero times zero point nine five to the tenth.
That's one minus zero point nine five to the tenth, about one minus zero point five nine nine, which is zero point four zero one.
The mean number of defectives is n p, ten times zero point zero five, which is zero point five.
The variance is n p q, ten times zero point zero five times zero point nine five, which is zero point four seven five.
Notice the variance, zero point four seven five, is below the mean, zero point five, exactly as a binomial requires.
The result is a nice reality check: even a five percent defect rate gives roughly a forty percent chance of catching at least one defective in ten. Small per-item risks accumulate fast.
A parameter-recovery problem, and the trick is one clean division.
The mean and variance of a binomial variable are four and two. Find n, p, and the probability of exactly two successes.
A binomial is completely determined by just two numbers, n and p, so mean and variance are exactly enough to pin it down.
Divide variance by mean: n p q over n p leaves q, which is two over four, one half. So p is one minus q, also one half.
Then from mean equals n p equals four, with p one half, n is four divided by one half, which is eight.
So X follows B of eight comma one half, and probability of exactly two is eight choose two times one half to the eighth, which is twenty eight over two hundred fifty six, or seven over sixty four.
Cross-check the given data: variance is eight times one half times one half, which is two, and the mean is four. They match, and variance is below mean as required.
The whole trick is to divide variance by mean first, which hands you q in a single step.
A J E E Advanced problem on the mode: the most probable number of successes.
An archer hits the bull's-eye with probability zero point eight on each shot and fires six independent shots. Find the most probable number of bull's-eyes, and the probability of achieving it.
Here n is six and p is zero point eight, so n plus one times p is seven times zero point eight, which is five point six — not an integer.
When that quantity isn't an integer, the mode is its floor, so the mode is five.
The probability of five hits is six choose five times zero point eight to the fifth times zero point two, which is about zero point three nine three.
Here's the insight: the mean is n p, four point eight, yet the single most likely count is five.
Mean and mode need not coincide, and the mode formula pins the peak of the distribution directly.
Where does the mode formula come from? Look at the ratio of consecutive probabilities.

That ratio is n minus r plus one, times p, over r times q. The probabilities keep rising while the ratio exceeds one and start falling once it drops below one, so the peak sits at the largest r where the climb is still happening.
Five traps sink the most marks on binomial questions, so let's name them.
Pitfall one: forcing the binomial formula onto trials that are dependent, like draws without replacement.
There the success probability shifts on each draw, so the setup is simply not binomial.
Pitfall two: swapping p and q, or equivalently r and n minus r.
Successes get p raised to r; failures get q raised to n minus r. Naming success clearly up front prevents this.
Pitfall three: believing the variance can exceed the mean.
For a binomial, n p q is always less than n p. A binomial with variance above the mean signals inconsistent data.
Pitfall four: taking the long road to at least one by summing every term, instead of one minus q to the n.
Pitfall five: dropping the n choose r factor, or miscomputing it — for example forgetting the n minus r factorial in the denominator. Always include it and evaluate it carefully.
Three reflexes cover the bulk of exam binomial questions. Burn them in.
First: any at-least or at-most question should trigger the complement reflex, choosing whichever side has fewer terms.
The cleanest case: probability of at least one is one minus probability of zero.
Second: whenever you're given a mean and variance and asked for n and p, divide variance by mean first.
That hands you q in one step; then p is one minus q, and n is the mean divided by p.
<whisper>Third: when you need several consecutive probabilities, compute probability of zero once, then walk up.</whisper>
Use the ratio of consecutive probabilities: n minus r plus one, times p, over r times q.
Each next probability is just the previous one times that simple factor — far quicker than recomputing the whole term every time.

First, the definition: probability of E given F is probability of E-and-F over probability of F, valid whenever the probability of F isn't zero.
Multiply both sides by probability of F and the definition turns into something you'll use everywhere, the multiplication theorem.
Probability of E-and-F equals probability of F times probability of E given F; or, conditioning the other way, probability of E times probability of F given E.
Both give the same intersection, so pick the direction whose conditional is easier to find. That choice alone saves time in exams.
For three events, chain them: probability of E-and-F-and-G is probability of E, times F given E, times G given E-and-F.
The pattern is clean: each new event is conditioned on everything that came before it.
One handy property: the complement of E given F is just one minus probability of E given F.
That works because a conditional probability is a genuine probability; it always sits between zero and one.
Here is the toolkit for this subtopic — three formulas that do all the work.
First, the partition. Your causes must be disjoint, so they never overlap; exhaustive, so they cover everything; and each must have positive probability.
In symbols, the causes' union is the whole sample space, and any two distinct causes have empty intersection.
Total Probability: the probability of A is the sum, over all causes, of each cause's prior times the likelihood of A under it.
That's the forward direction: you weight each cause's likelihood by its prior and add them up.
Bayes: the posterior for cause E-i is that cause's prior times likelihood, divided by the full sum over all causes.
And the denominator is not a new quantity; it's exactly probability of A from Total Probability.
In words: posterior equals prior times likelihood, over the probability of the evidence.
Let's lay out the formula toolkit for this subtopic, starting with the basics.
A distribution is valid only when every probability is legal and they add to one.
In symbols: each p-i is at least zero, and the sum of all p-i is one.
The mean, or expectation, is the sum of each value times its probability. It's the probability-weighted centre.
Say it out loud so you never slip: weighted, not plain. Frequent values pull the mean toward themselves.
You'll also need expectation of X squared: the sum of each value squared times its probability.
That quantity is what feeds the variance, so accumulate it in the same table pass as the mean.
And to pin an unknown constant k in a distribution, set the sum of the probabilities to one and solve for k, then check every probability stays legal.
Now variance, standard deviation, and the linear-transformation rules that J E E leans on.
Variance in its definition form is the sum of squared deviations from the mean, each weighted by its probability.
The equivalent computational form is expectation of X squared, minus the square of expectation of X.
The two are equal; reach for the second one in exams because it's far faster on decimals.
Standard deviation is just the square root of the variance.
For a linear change: expectation of a X plus b is a times expectation of X, plus b.
And variance of a X plus b is a squared times variance of X.
Note the plus b shifts the mean but never affects the variance, while the scale factor a enters squared.
One permanent sanity check: variance is always greater than or equal to zero. A negative answer means you dropped the square on mu.

X takes one, two, three, four, with probability of X equal to k times x. Find k, then the mean and variance, then handle Y equals two X minus one.
First k: the probabilities must sum to one, so k times the total one plus two plus three plus four is ten k equals one, giving k equal to one tenth.
Check the probabilities: one tenth, two tenths, three tenths, four tenths all lie between zero and one, so k is valid.
The mean is the sum of x times k x, which is one plus four plus nine plus sixteen, over ten, equal to thirty over ten, or three.
Expectation of X squared is one plus eight plus twenty seven plus sixty four, over ten, which is one hundred over ten, or ten.
So variance is ten minus three squared, which is one.
Now for Y equals two X minus one, don't rebuild a table; use the linear rules.
Expectation of Y is two times three minus one, which is five; and variance of Y is two squared times one, which is four.

Read the result: doubling X, the factor a equals two, quadrupled the spread, while the minus one shift moved the mean but left the variance untouched. That's why a enters squared and the constant drops out.
Let's derive the binomial formula, because reading it as three meaningful pieces makes it almost impossible to misremember.
Fix one specific pattern of r successes and n minus r failures — say successes on the first r trials, and failures on all the rest.
Because the trials are independent, the probability of that exact sequence is p multiplied r times, then q multiplied n minus r times: p to the r, times q to the n minus r.
Now the crucial observation: every arrangement of r successes among the n trials carries the same probability, p to the r q to the n minus r. Only the order differs.
The number of distinct arrangements is the number of ways to choose which r trials are the successes, namely n choose r.
Since those arrangements are mutually exclusive, we add their equal probabilities, giving probability of X equals r is n choose r times p to the r times q to the n minus r.
That addition of equal, mutually exclusive arrangements is where the n choose r factor comes from — it's not decoration.
As a check, sum over all r from zero to n. By the Binomial Theorem, that's q plus p, all to the n, which is one to the n, which is one.

Let's consolidate the binomial toolkit, starting with the setup.
A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes: success with probability p, failure with probability q, which is one minus p.
For a count to be binomial, four conditions must hold: a fixed number of trials n, independent trials, exactly two outcomes, and a constant success probability p.
When they hold, we write X follows B of n comma p.
The distribution is: probability of X equals r is n choose r times p to the r times q to the n minus r, for r running from zero to n.
There are exactly n plus one probabilities, one for each possible count r.
They automatically sum to one, because they are the terms of q plus p, all to the n.
And the shape: the distribution is symmetric exactly when p is one half, and grows more skewed as p moves away from one half.
Now the moments and the exam shortcuts.
Mean is n p, variance is n p q, and standard deviation is the square root of n p q.
Carry this always: the variance is strictly less than the mean, because q is below one.
The mode, the most probable number of successes, is the integer r satisfying n plus one, times p, minus one, is at most r, which is at most n plus one times p.
When n plus one times p is not an integer, the mode is simply the floor of that quantity — round down.
For at least one success, use the complement: one minus q to the n. Never sum all the terms.
That's a reflex worth burning in — at least one is always one minus the probability of none.
To recover parameters from a given mean and variance, divide variance by mean to get q, then p is one minus q, and n is the mean divided by p.
That order matters: get q first from the ratio, and the rest falls out in one step each.
